t: Listen to a talk in an architecture class.
Medieval builders wanted cathedrals with very high walls and huge windows, to fill the interior with light.
But a tall stone wall with big holes in it is weak.
The heavy stone roof pushes the top of the wall outward, and the wall can collapse.
Their solution was the flying buttress, an arm of stone built outside the wall that leans against it and carries that outward push down to the ground.
Imagine a person leaning a hand against a wobbly bookcase to keep it upright.
With the buttresses taking the load, the walls themselves no longer had to be thick, and builders could fill them with stained glass.
Notre-Dame in Paris is a well-known example, and its buttresses were added partly because cracks appeared in the walls.
